items.name: Request
items.doc: `raw_headers` is exactly the CRLF-separated "name: value" lines this request's header block was made of, unparsed -- not a map[str]str. Building a map costs an allocation for the map plus roughly two more per header, on every request, whether or not anything ever reads a header; most requests never do. `header`/`header_or` scan this directly (strings.find_field, no allocation for the search itself); `headers()` builds a map from it on demand for a caller that genuinely wants one. Constructed only by `parse`/`read` (off the wire) or `request` (validated, from a map) -- never assign this field directly from unvalidated bytes; a value containing "\r\n" inside a hand-built block is a second header no map ever held.

items.name: WireFrame
items.doc: `read` couples two things that only sometimes belong together: filling the caller's buffer and framing what's in it. serve_conn needs the split for frame dispatch: read_frame frames with the same scans/errors/rules as read, but returns the parsed head (method/path strs, header block, body) instead of a Request -- so the router matches on strs with no raw copy, no rescan, no second slice. Offsets stay for Frame callers and tests; the serve path does not use them.

items.name: Frame
items.doc: The request WITHOUT materialising method/path/version strs: framing offsets only. `read`/`serve` use this when they only route on the raw path bytes (see path_matches below); `parse` keeps returning strs for callers that actually need them.

items.name: header
items.sig: fn header(r: Request, name: str) -> opt[str]

items.name: header_or
items.sig: fn header_or(r: Request, name: str, fallback: str) -> str
items.doc: header()'s two real call sites (Ctx.header in zokor, the WebSocket handshake) are both `header(...) ?? fallback` already -- this is that, without the opt allocation `??` unwraps.

items.name: headers
items.doc: Every header a request carries, as a map -- built fresh on each call by scanning raw_headers once. Nothing in either repo iterates a request's headers today (confirmed by grep), which is what makes "built on demand" the right default over a cached field: a cache nothing reads is pure cost. Walks the same line shape scan_headers does, for a different reason (that one validates and extracts two offsets; this one assumes an already-valid block and extracts every name and value) -- kept as two functions rather than one parameterized by what to do with each line, which would obscure both to save repeating six lines.

items.name: request
items.sig: fn request(method: str, path: str, version: str,
items.doc: Builds a Request from a map the way the eager parser builds one off the wire: a header name or value may not contain CR or LF (an application- or test-constructed header gets no such check for free the way one read off the wire does -- this is where that rule lives for this path), and a name may not contain the colon that separates it from its value on the wire. Both are a real hazard, not a theoretical one, now that raw_headers is what a request's headers actually are: a value containing "\r\n" would be concatenated straight into the block below as a SECOND header line -- injection -- if it weren't rejected first.

items.name: parse_frame
items.doc: Framing offsets for one request inside `raw`, with NOTHING materialised: no method/path/version strs, no header copies. The request line is validated (two spaces, HTTP/1.x token); the header block is validated by scan_headers; the body is framed by frame(). Callers that need strs (logging, tests) use parse(); the server path matches/routes directly on these offsets -- see path_matches and method_is below -- so the ~10 framing strs per request never exist.

items.name: method_is
items.sig: fn method_is(raw: bytes, f: Frame, want: str) -> bool
items.doc: Is this frame's method exactly `want` (e.g. "GET"), compared in place -- no method str is ever built. Takes a line_end int (not a Frame) so both Frame and WireFrame callers share it.

items.name: method_is_at
items.sig: fn method_is_at(raw: bytes, line_end: int, want: str) -> bool

items.name: path_is
items.sig: fn path_is(raw: bytes, f: Frame, want: str) -> bool
items.doc: Is this frame's path exactly `want` (bytes compared in place, query string ignored -- matches path.strip_query semantics)? No path str. The two hot paths (`/` and `/users/`-prefixed) compare inline with no to_bytes at all; anything else falls through to the general compare, which still costs one to_bytes of `want`. Route fpaths could precompute that bytes once at registration -- the next step if `/users/:id` still shows hot after this.

items.name: path_is_at
items.sig: fn path_is_at(raw: bytes, line_end: int, want: str) -> bool

items.name: serialize_builder
items.doc: The old builder path, kept for the differential test: must stay byte-identical to serialize_sized() above for every shape.

items.name: serialize_sized
items.doc: Serialize with a handful of allocations, not ~40: size the response first (status line + headers + framing + body, all cheap integer arithmetic over lengths -- see emit_len below), allocate exactly that many bytes with strings.bytes_zero (one header plus one buffer -- no throwaway str), then fill by slice assignment. The old builder path stays below as serialize_builder for the differential test; this is what `serialize` and `write`'s fallback call, so an oversized response costs a few allocations instead of ~40.  The remaining handful is load-bearing, not waste: one to_bytes per fill_str piece (the str->bytes copy the compiler cannot fuse), one filtered-extra list, and the response_conn scan's own line strs. Counting them is what keeps this honest -- see the probe notes.

items.name: escape_json_bytes
items.doc: The escaped form of `msg` as bytes, for a caller that already holds bytes and wants the quoted payload without a str in between.

items.name: with_header
items.sig: fn with_header(r: Response, name: str, value: str) -> Response

items.name: without_header
items.sig: fn without_header(r: Response, name: str) -> Response

items.name: wants_close
items.doc: Whether the connection should close after answering `r`: HTTP/1.1 stays open unless the client sent `Connection: close`, HTTP/1.0 closes unless it sent `Connection: keep-alive` (either case-insensitive, OWS trimmed; with the header repeated, the one `header()` returns decides). Allocates nothing.

items.name: version_flag_of
items.doc: The int-flag twin, for callers holding a version str rather than a Head (read_frame's WireFrame.version). Same rules; the block is passed explicitly because there is no Head in scope.

items.name: read_frame
items.sig: fn read_frame(c: &mut link, buf: wire, filled: int,
items.doc: read_frame: read's framing, plus the parsed head the router matches on. Implemented INSIDE read's loop shape (not as read-plus-copy): read compacts the buffer before returning, so after read there is no head left to copy -- buf[0..filled] is the NEXT request. This duplicates read's loop deliberately (same scans, same errors, same close rules), and the duplication is the contract: any change to read's framing must land here too.  What differs from read: on a complete frame the method/path strs and the header block + body are COPIED OUT of the wire ONCE -- the same strs + copies read already pays (hd.method/path, hd.headers, hd.body) -- and NO separate message copy is made. The old shape did to_bytes(buf[0..end]) PLUS parse_frame over the copy PLUS wants_close_scan over the copy: a full second framing pass and a whole-message copy per request. Now the WireFrame carries what the router needs directly: method/path strs for the enum + Request build, headers/body slices for the Ctx. Routing matches on strs (==), never on raw bytes -- no path_is_at rescan, no per-route to_bytes. The message copy is gone entirely.  Chunked bodies: hd.body IS the reassembled copy (one alloc the old path also spent); the WireFrame body is that copy directly. Three deadlines, not one, because "how long should this wait" has three different honest answers depending on what the connection is doing: idle_deadline while nothing has arrived at all yet (a kept- alive connection between requests, or a fresh one that never sends anything -- this is the one that should be generous, since a real client legitimately sits idle between requests); header_deadline once bytes have started arriving but the request line and headers aren't complete yet; body_deadline once the headers are in but a declared body hasn't fully arrived. header_deadline and body_deadline are both the tight, slow-loris-shaped ones -- a client that has started a request and then trickles it in a byte at a time is not the same risk as one that hasn't sent anything yet, and idle_deadline being long must not become an amplifier for that. Recomputed fresh every loop iteration rather than tracked as a separate flag: frame_head_wire's own re-parse of the same (only ever growing) buffer already answers "is the header complete yet" idempotently, so re-deriving which phase this recv is in from that costs nothing extra and can't drift out of sync with it.

items.name: read
items.sig: fn read(c: &mut link, buf: wire, filled: int, deadline: until) -> result[Incoming, str]

items.name: StaticBody
items.doc: serialize()'s GC allocations (~40 of them for a typical response, see serialize()'s own comment) replaced with two passes over the caller's own arena: size, then fill. If the response is larger than what's left of the arena, falls back to serialize() + send_bytes rather than letting a.wire(need) past capacity kill the task -- a slow response stays a slow response instead of becoming a dropped connection.  Responses with exactly the `text_response` shape (one content-type, nothing else) take the fixed fast path above: no map iteration, no integer str, no intermediate bytes. Anything else uses the general `emit` below, unchanged. A static route's answer: status, content type, and body -- no Response struct, no extra list, nothing to shape-check. serve_conn gets one from serve_static and hands it straight to write_static, which sends the PREBUILT keep-alive rendering (assembled once at registration -- see static_render below) with one wire alloc and one memcpy. The static snapshot lives on the Route (see router.sl); this is just the per-request view of it.

items.name: write_static
items.sig: fn write_static(c: &mut link, b: StaticBody, a: &mut arena,
items.doc: The static emit: the keep-alive rendering is prebuilt, not emitted. Hot path (HTTP/1.1 keep-alive, which is every wrk/ab request): one wire, one memcpy, one send -- no probe pass, no Response struct, no map, no integer str, no per-piece puts. The close variant (HTTP/1.0, Connection: close) is rare and pays the emit cost below; it never touches the hot path.

items.name: static_render
items.sig: fn static_render(status: i32, content_type: str, body: bytes) -> bytes
items.doc: The keep-alive rendering, assembled ONCE at registration: status line, one content-type, content-length, connection, blank line, body -- the exact bytes write_static memcpys per request. status_text_of covers the statuses static routes return; the fallback ("OK") matches write_static's own close variant above, so the two can never disagree on a reason phrase.

items.sig: fn write(c: &mut link, r: Response, a: &mut arena, deadline: until) -> result[int, fault]

items.doc: `text_response` with a BYTES body: same shape, no `to_bytes` copy. The hot path (zokor's JSON renderers, static bodies) already holds bytes; forcing them through str and back cost a full copy plus the literal's own allocation on every response.

items.sig: fn text_response(status: i32, status_text: str, content_type: str,

items.name: W_RAW
items.sig: let W_RAW = 0;       // pre-built frames, not flow controlled
items.doc: ---- writer messages -------------------------------------------------  Everything the writer task needs arrives on ONE channel, tagged.  When this was written slang had no `select`, so a writer watching both "here is a response" and "the peer granted more window" on two channels could only ever block on one of them. `select` exists now and would compile -- but the single tagged stream is still the better design here, and stays. Two channels would make the ORDER between a grant and a body a race the writer has to reason about; one channel makes it the order they were sent, for free, and leaves the writer an ordinary state machine with a single blocking point.

items.name: W_BODY
items.sig: let W_BODY = 1;      // a response: HEADERS now, DATA as window allows

items.name: W_GRANT
items.sig: let W_GRANT = 2;     // peer's WINDOW_UPDATE: `n` octets to `stream`

items.name: W_INITIAL
items.sig: let W_INITIAL = 3;   // peer's SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE is now `n`

items.name: W_MAXFRAME
items.sig: let W_MAXFRAME = 4;  // peer's SETTINGS_MAX_FRAME_SIZE is now `n`

items.name: grant_msg
items.sig: fn grant_msg(stream: int, n: int) -> WMsg

items.name: response_msg
items.sig: fn response_msg(stream: int, status: str, extra: [Header],
items.doc: Build a response. The body is handed over UNFRAMED: the writer owns the peer's window and its max frame size, so it -- not the handler -- decides how the body is cut into DATA frames and when each may go.

items.name: Limits
items.doc: ---- deadlines -------------------------------------------------------  Four separate budgets, in nanoseconds, because they defend against four different peers and want wildly different numbers.  `idle` is the generous one on purpose: an HTTP/2 connection sitting open with no streams is completely normal -- that is the whole point of connection reuse -- so timing it out aggressively breaks correct clients. `request` is the strict one: once a client has started a request it must finish it, and dribbling DATA forever is exactly the slowloris shape.

items.name: is_timeout
items.doc: The reserved error string net.recv_until / net.send_until return when a deadline passes. Exposed as a predicate so callers can react to a slow peer (GOAWAY with ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM) differently from a broken one, without hardcoding the text.

items.name: MAX_HEADER_FIELDS
items.doc: Our own limits, advertised in SETTINGS and enforced on receipt.

items.name: RESET_BURST
items.doc: ---- Rapid Reset (CVE-2023-44487) ------------------------------------  A peer opens a stream and immediately RST_STREAMs it. From its side the stream is closed the instant it opens, so a concurrency limit never sees it -- while the server has already done the HPACK decode and, in most designs, started the work. Repeat and the server is driven at whatever rate the attacker can write frames.  Cancelling a request IS legitimate: a browser navigating away resets its in-flight streams, and a client that gives up on a slow endpoint should. So a flat "no resets" rule would break correct clients. What is not legitimate is resetting nearly everything you open, forever.  Hence a burst plus a ratio: RESET_BURST cancellations are free, and after that a peer whose resets outnumber half of what it opened is ending the connection. A browser that abandons a page load trips neither; a Rapid Reset flood resets every stream it opens, so it trips both the moment the burst is spent.

items.name: our_settings
items.doc: Our SETTINGS: a modest frame size, and push disabled because server push is deprecated and no current client wants it.

items.name: gate
items.doc: ---- the stream gate -------------------------------------------------  The connection layer cannot cap concurrency on its own: it does not spawn the handlers, the CALLER does. (slang has function values now, so handing it a callback would compile -- but that only moves the same question inside, and the answer would still be this.) So the bound lives in a token channel the caller holds, and this is the mechanism plus the vocabulary for it.  A gate is a chan[bool] holding `n` tokens. gate_enter takes one and blocks when none are left; gate_leave puts one back. That blocking IS the backpressure -- the reader stops pulling frames while every slot is busy, which is the correct answer to "more work than I can do", and far better than the alternative measured before this existed: 3002 concurrent handler tasks from a peer we had told our limit was 100.  It also solves shutdown. Closing the writer channel while handlers are still in flight panics them with "send on closed channel", and nothing else could tell whether any were left. gate_drain waits for every token to come home, so the close is safe by construction.  The one rule: gate_leave must run on EVERY path out of a handler, including error returns. A lost token permanently shrinks the connection's capacity, and losing all of them wedges that connection (only that one -- the failure is bounded and visible, not a crash).

items.name: gate_drain
items.doc: Wait until every handler has finished, by collecting all `n` tokens. Call before chan_close on the writer channel.

items.name: Transport
items.doc: ---- transport -------------------------------------------------------  h2 runs over cleartext TCP (h2c, prior knowledge) or over TLS, and the two are reached through different runtime calls: net.recv_until on an fd, net.tls_recv_until on an SSL handle. Everything above this point is identical either way, so the difference is confined to one struct and two functions rather than duplicated through the whole layer.  This matters beyond tidiness: browsers speak HTTP/2 ONLY over TLS with ALPN, so a connection layer that can only do fds cannot serve a browser at all, however conformant the rest of it is.

items.name: transport_fd
items.doc: h2c: cleartext, prior knowledge. curl --http2-prior-knowledge, and Go's http2.Transport with AllowHTTP.

items.name: transport_tls
items.doc: h2 over TLS. The handle comes from net.tls_accept, and the caller is responsible for having negotiated "h2" via ALPN first -- see alpn_is_h2 below.

items.name: alpn_is_h2
items.doc: RFC 7301 §3.1: the peer either selected "h2" or it did not. A server that advertised h2 and http/1.1 must look, because a browser offered both and may well have picked http/1.1 -- feeding an HTTP/1.1 client into this layer produces "bad connection preface", which is true but unhelpful.

items.name: read_frame
items.sig: fn read_frame(r: Reader, t: Transport, max_frame: int, u: until)
items.doc: Pull bytes until at least one complete frame is buffered, then return it and keep the remainder. Note the `&mut *c` at every site below that forwards this borrow: passing `c` directly MOVES it, so the second call would fail with "use of moved value". Reborrowing keeps the caller's borrow usable.  `u` bounds the WHOLE call, not each recv: a peer that sends one octet every second must still finish the frame inside the budget, which is what makes this a slowloris defence rather than a keepalive check. Pass until_never() only where blocking forever is genuinely intended.

items.name: accept_preface
items.sig: fn accept_preface(r: Reader, t: Transport, wch: chan[WMsg], u: until)
items.doc: Verify the 24-byte client connection preface and send ours.

items.name: read_request
items.sig: fn read_request(cn: Conn, r: Reader, t: Transport, wch: chan[WMsg],
items.doc: Read frames until one complete request has arrived.  Two clocks, switched at the first HEADERS. Before it the connection is idle and gets the generous `idle` budget, refreshed by each control frame that arrives -- a client PINGing a kept-alive connection is behaving correctly and must not be disconnected. After it the strict `request` budget applies to the request as a WHOLE and is never refreshed, so no amount of dribbled DATA or CONTINUATION can extend it.

items.name: writer_task
items.sig: fn writer_task(t: Transport, wch: chan[WMsg], write_ns: int)
items.doc: Owns the write side, and with it the peer's send windows.  Flow control has to live here rather than in the handlers. The window is a property of the CONNECTION, shared by every concurrent stream, so no handler can decide on its own whether it may send -- and the WINDOW_UPDATE that grants credit arrives on the read side, in a different task entirely. Routing both into this one task is what lets the accounting be correct without a lock at all. slang does have a mutex now, but reaching for one here would be the worse design: it would serialise the writers without making the window arithmetic any less shared.  A blocked stream parks its BODY here, not its task: the handler hands the response over and moves on, so a peer with a tiny window costs a queue entry rather than a live task.

items.name: respond
items.sig: fn respond(cn: Conn, wch: chan[WMsg], stream: int, status: str,
items.doc: Enqueue a response for `stream`. Every write on the connection goes through the writer task, so there is deliberately no direct-write variant: one would be able to interleave with a handler mid-frame.

items.name: send_reset
items.sig: fn send_reset(wch: chan[WMsg], stream: int, code: int)

items.name: send_goaway

items.name: T_DATA
items.doc: Frame types (RFC 9113 §6). PUSH_PROMISE is parsed but never sent: server push is deprecated and no major client accepts it any more.

items.name: FLAG_END_STREAM
items.doc: Flags. The same bit means different things per frame type, which is why these are named by type: 0x1 is END_STREAM on DATA/HEADERS but ACK on SETTINGS/PING.

items.name: E_NO_ERROR
items.doc: Error codes (RFC 9113 §7).

items.name: S_HEADER_TABLE_SIZE
items.doc: Settings parameters (RFC 9113 §6.5.2).

items.name: preface
items.doc: The connection preface a client must send first (RFC 9113 §3.4).

items.sig: fn be16(b: bytes, off: int) -> int

items.name: header_bytes

items.doc: Decode one frame at `off`. `max_frame` is our advertised SETTINGS_MAX_FRAME_SIZE: a peer exceeding it is a connection error, and checking here keeps a bogus length from driving a huge allocation.

items.name: strip_padding
items.sig: fn strip_padding(payload: bytes, flags: int) -> result[bytes, str]

items.name: decode_block
items.sig: fn decode_block(d: Decoder, b: bytes, max_headers: int)
items.doc: Decode one complete header block. `max_headers` caps how many fields a peer may send: without it a small compressed block can expand into an unbounded list, which is the HPACK bomb.

items.name: encode_header
items.sig: fn encode_header(name: str, value: str) -> bytes

items.name: Table
items.doc: A decoder's dynamic table. Bounded by `cap` octets, where each entry costs len(name) + len(value) + 32 (RFC 7541 §4.1); the constant accounts for per-entry overhead so a peer cannot exhaust memory with many tiny headers.

items.name: table_add
items.sig: fn table_add(t: Table, name: str, value: str)

items.name: read_int
items.sig: fn read_int(b: bytes, off: int, prefix_bits: int) -> result[IntRead, str]

items.name: write_int
items.sig: fn write_int(v: int, prefix_bits: int, first: int) -> bytes
items.doc: `first` supplies the bits ABOVE the prefix (the representation tag).

items.name: read_string
items.sig: fn read_string(h: Huff, b: bytes, off: int) -> result[StrRead, str]

items.name: write_string
items.doc: Always emitted as a raw literal, never Huffman-coded. That is fully legal (the H bit says which), costs a few bytes per response, and avoids shipping an encoder table for a saving the transport layer mostly recovers anyway.

items.name: huff_decode
items.sig: fn huff_decode(h: Huff, src: bytes) -> result[bytes, str]
items.doc: Decode a Huffman-coded byte string to BYTES, not str.  Returning str here would be a silent data-loss bug: symbol 0 is NUL, and to_str truncates there, so a value containing \x00 came back empty. Header field values are byte sequences on the wire; the caller decides whether to reject NUL (read_string does) rather than having the codec quietly drop everything after it.  Padding rules (RFC 7541 §5.2) are enforced rather than ignored: the tail must be fewer than 8 bits, must be all ones, and must not encode a symbol. A decoder that skips these accepts streams a conforming one rejects, which is how HPACK implementations end up disagreeing.

items.name: huff_counts
items.doc: counts[l] = number of codes of length l (index 0..30; 0..4 are zero)

items.name: huff_symbols
items.doc: symbols in canonical order: all 5-bit codes, then 6-bit, and so on

items.name: static_find
items.sig: fn static_find(name: str, value: str) -> int
items.doc: Index of an exact name+value match, or 0. Used by the encoder to send a one-byte indexed field for the common cases (:status 200, :method GET) instead of a literal.

items.name: static_find_name
items.doc: Index of any entry with this name, or 0 -- lets the encoder reference a known name and send only the value as a literal.

items.doc: Record a Set-Cookie line as if `url` had sent it, under exactly the rules a real response gets -- the same function does both. For a program restoring a session it saved, or seeding a jar for a test. Has no effect unless enable_cookies was called, the same as a response would not.

items.name: cookies
items.doc: What the jar would send to `url` right now. For inspection and tests; a request does this itself.

items.name: close_idle
items.doc: Close every idle connection now. A long-lived service does not need this -- idle_timeout reaps them -- but a program about to exit, or a test counting connections, does.

items.name: Notification
items.doc: A NOTIFY delivered to a connection that LISTENs on its channel.

items.name: Arg
items.doc: A query parameter. Build one with arg_text, arg_int, arg_float, arg_bool, arg_bytes or arg_null.

items.name: Rows
items.doc: A buffered result. Read cells with get_text / get_int / get_float / get_bool / get_bytes, by row and column index; col() finds an index by name.

items.name: parse_url
items.doc: postgres://user:password@host:port/database?sslmode=require  Recognised parameters: sslmode, sslrootcert, application_name, host and port. Any other parameter is an error rather than ignored: a misspelt "sslmdoe=require" that was silently dropped would connect in the clear, and nothing would ever say so.  sslmode: disable      cleartext. require      TLS, certificate and hostname verified. verify-full  the same as require (the libpq spelling of it). prefer, allow, verify-ca are refused. The first two fall back to cleartext when TLS fails, which is exactly what an attacker in the middle would arrange; verify-ca checks the chain but not the host.  With no sslmode the default is "require" -- except for a loopback host, where it is "disable", because traffic that never leaves the machine gains nothing from TLS and a local development server almost never has it configured.  A Unix-domain socket is named by its DIRECTORY, as libpq does: either percent-encoded as the host (postgres://app@%2Fvar%2Frun%2Fpostgresql/db) or as ?host=/var/run/postgresql. The socket file is <dir>/.s.PGSQL.<port>. Postgres does not use TLS over one, so sslmode defaults to disable and asking for require is an error.

items.name: sqlstate
items.doc: The SQLSTATE of an error returned by this package, or "" when the error did not come from the server (a dial failure, a timeout).  if pg.sqlstate(e) == "23505" { /* unique_violation */ }

items.name: Scram
items.doc: One SCRAM-SHA-256 exchange (RFC 5802, RFC 7677), as pure functions of its inputs, so the published test vector can check it.

items.name: connect
items.sig: fn connect(url: str, deadline: until) -> result[Conn, str]

items.name: connect_config
items.sig: fn connect_config(cfg: Config, deadline: until) -> result[Conn, str]
items.doc: The deadline bounds the whole connection: the lookup, the TCP connect, the TLS handshake and the startup and authentication exchange.

items.name: close
items.doc: Ends the session politely (Terminate) and closes the socket. Safe to call on a broken or already-closed connection.

items.name: usable
items.doc: Is the connection still usable? False once it has been closed or has broken; a false Conn only ever returns errors.

items.name: in_transaction
items.doc: Inside a transaction block (including a failed one that still needs ROLLBACK)?

items.name: server_param
items.sig: fn server_param(c: Conn, name: str) -> opt[str]
items.doc: A server setting reported at startup or after SET: "server_version", "TimeZone", "standard_conforming_strings", ...

items.name: arg_float
items.doc: Sent as the shortest text that reads back as exactly this float: to_str's six significant digits would round it.

items.name: arg_bytes
items.doc: Sent in binary, so any byte values -- NULs included -- arrive intact. For a bytea column.

items.name: query
items.sig: fn query(c: Conn, sql: str, args: [Arg], deadline: until)
items.doc: Runs one query with parameters ($1, $2, ...) through the extended protocol: the values travel separately from the SQL text, so they can never be parsed as SQL. Returns every row, buffered; for a result too big to hold at once, use stream().

items.name: exec
items.sig: fn exec(c: Conn, sql: str, deadline: until) -> result[int, str]
items.doc: Runs SQL with no parameters through the simple protocol, which accepts several statements separated by semicolons -- a migration, a schema. Returns the rows affected by the last statement. Rows a statement returns are read and discarded.  Never build `sql` from untrusted input: use query() and parameters.

items.name: stream
items.sig: fn stream(c: Conn, sql: str, args: [Arg], deadline: until)

items.name: next_row
items.sig: fn next_row(c: Conn, rows: Rows, deadline: until) -> result[bool, str]
items.doc: Reads the next row of a stream into `rows` (at index 0). Returns false once there are no more; rows.affected and rows.tag are set then.

items.name: stream_close
items.sig: fn stream_close(c: Conn, rows: Rows, deadline: until) -> result[bool, str]
items.doc: Ends a stream early. The server is asked to cancel the query first -- and that request is seen through before the rest is drained, so it can never land on a LATER query on this connection -- then whatever it had already sent is read and dropped. The connection is then free.

items.name: copy_in_start
items.sig: fn copy_in_start(c: Conn, sql: str, deadline: until) -> result[bool, str]
items.doc: Starts COPY ... FROM STDIN. Send data with copy_in_send, then finish with copy_in_end -- or copy_in_abort, which rolls the COPY back.

items.name: copy_in_send
items.sig: fn copy_in_send(c: Conn, data: bytes, deadline: until) -> result[bool, str]
items.doc: Sends COPY data. It need not end on a row boundary; the server reassembles it. An error in the data is reported by copy_in_end.

items.name: copy_in_end
items.sig: fn copy_in_end(c: Conn, deadline: until) -> result[int, str]
items.doc: Ends the COPY. Returns the number of rows loaded, or the server's error about the data -- in which case nothing was loaded.

items.name: copy_in_abort
items.sig: fn copy_in_abort(c: Conn, reason: str, deadline: until) -> result[bool, str]
items.doc: Abandons the COPY: the server discards everything sent. Ok once the server has confirmed; its "COPY from stdin failed" is the expected answer, not an error.

items.name: copy_from
items.sig: fn copy_from(c: Conn, sql: str, data: bytes, deadline: until)
items.doc: COPY ... FROM STDIN in one call. Returns the rows loaded.  pg.copy_from(c, "COPY users (id, email) FROM STDIN (FORMAT csv)", to_bytes("1,a@example.com\n2,b@example.com\n"), dl)

items.name: copy_out_start
items.sig: fn copy_out_start(c: Conn, sql: str, deadline: until) -> result[bool, str]
items.doc: Starts COPY ... TO STDOUT. Read it with copy_out_next.

items.name: copy_out_next
items.sig: fn copy_out_next(c: Conn, deadline: until) -> result[opt[bytes], str]
items.doc: The next piece of COPY output -- in text and CSV formats, one row -- or none when it is complete.

items.name: copy_to
items.sig: fn copy_to(c: Conn, sql: str, deadline: until) -> result[bytes, str]
items.doc: COPY ... TO STDOUT in one call, buffered (up to the 256 MiB result limit; stream a larger one with copy_out_start / copy_out_next).

items.name: listen
items.sig: fn listen(c: Conn, channel: str, deadline: until) -> result[bool, str]

items.name: unlisten
items.sig: fn unlisten(c: Conn, channel: str, deadline: until) -> result[bool, str]
items.doc: "*" stops listening on every channel.

items.name: notify
items.sig: fn notify(c: Conn, channel: str, payload: str, deadline: until)

items.name: wait_notification
items.doc: The oldest queued notification, or waits for one until the deadline: none then. Unlike every other call, reaching the deadline here is not an error and does not break the connection -- waiting is the point.

items.name: col
items.sig: fn col(rows: Rows, name: str) -> int
items.doc: The index of the column called `name`. Panics if there is none: the query and the code reading it disagree, which is a bug, not a condition to handle.

items.name: is_null
items.sig: fn is_null(rows: Rows, r: int, c: int) -> bool

items.name: get_text
items.sig: fn get_text(rows: Rows, r: int, c: int) -> str

items.name: get_int

items.name: get_float
items.sig: fn get_float(rows: Rows, r: int, c: int) -> float
items.doc: float4, float8, numeric, and the integer types. A numeric too precise for a double is rounded; read it with get_text to keep every digit.

items.name: get_bool
items.sig: fn get_bool(rows: Rows, r: int, c: int) -> bool

items.name: Pool
items.doc: A bounded set of connections to one database, shared by any number of tasks.

items.name: new_pool
items.sig: fn new_pool(url: str, max_open: int) -> result[Pool, str]
items.doc: Parses the url; connects nothing until the first acquire.

items.name: acquire
items.sig: fn acquire(p: Pool, deadline: until) -> result[Conn, str]
items.doc: A connection for the caller's exclusive use, until release(). Prefer pool_query / pool_exec, which cannot forget to release; acquire is for a transaction, which needs several statements on one connection.

items.name: release
items.doc: Returns a connection to the pool. One that is broken, closed, or still inside a transaction is closed instead: handing an open transaction to the next caller would run its statements inside someone else's uncommitted work.

items.name: pool_query
items.sig: fn pool_query(p: Pool, sql: str, args: [Arg], deadline: until)

items.name: pool_exec
items.sig: fn pool_exec(p: Pool, sql: str, deadline: until) -> result[int, str]

items.name: pool_close
items.doc: Closes every idle connection. Connections in use are closed as they are released; acquire fails from now on.

items.name: REPLY_SIMPLE
items.doc: The five RESP2 reply types. A reply is always one of exactly one.

items.name: REPLY_BULK
items.sig: let REPLY_BULK = 3;     // $len\r\n<bytes> (bulk holds it, none when nil)

items.name: Decoded
items.doc: A decoded reply plus how many bytes of the input it consumed, so a connection holding a read buffer knows what to keep.

items.name: encode
items.doc:
Encode one command invocation as a RESP2 array of bulk strings: SET key value  ->  *3
$3
SET
$3
key
$5
value
 Takes already-encoded argument bytes, so binary-safe values pass through untouched. Pure: no I/O, no allocation beyond the result.

items.name: decode
items.doc: Decode one RESP2 reply from the front of `buf`. ok(none) means the buffer ends mid-message -- feed more bytes and retry. ok(some(d)) consumed d.consumed bytes; anything after them is the next message. err means the bytes violate the protocol: never retry on the same connection.

items.name: decode_at
items.sig: fn decode_at(buf: bytes, pos: int) -> result[opt[Decoded], str]
items.doc: Decode one reply starting at `pos` instead of 0, for readers that keep one long-lived buffer and an offset into it (see Conn): no slicing, so no per-recv copy of everything already buffered. consumed counts from `pos`.

items.name: slot
items.doc: The hash slot of a key, 0..16383. `{...}` hash tags force colocation: only what sits between the first `{` and the next `}` is hashed. Empty tags hash the whole key, and a `{` with no `}` is literal.

items.name: parse_url
items.doc: Parse redis://[[username:]password@]host[:port][/db][?sslmode=...]. rediss:// forces sslmode=require. Percent-escapes in credentials and database decode the same way pg's URLs do.

items.name: Conn
items.doc: One server connection: exactly one round trip in flight at a time, serialized by lock. A Conn is safe to share between tasks; every public call below takes the lock for its whole exchange.

items.name: connect_config
items.sig: fn connect_config(cfg: Config, deadline: until) -> result[Conn, str]
items.doc: Open a connection from a parsed Config and run the handshake (AUTH when a password is set, SELECT when db is not 0). The deadline covers everything: DNS, TCP connect, TLS upgrade, login.

items.name: connect
items.sig: fn connect(url: str, deadline: until) -> result[Conn, str]
items.doc: Open a connection from a URL. See parse_url for the shape.

items.name: do
items.sig: fn do(c: Conn, args: [bytes], deadline: until) -> result[Reply, str]
items.doc: Run one command: args[0] is the command name. Exactly one reply is consumed, so at most one command is ever in flight per Conn; hold no lock of your own -- this takes c.lock for the round trip. Refused inside MULTI: queued commands answer +QUEUED, which no typed shape could read -- use queue there.

items.name: close
items.doc: Shut the connection down. In-flight calls on other tasks finish (or hit their own deadlines) first; close waits for the lock.

items.name: usable
items.doc: True while commands may still be attempted: not closed, not broken. A server-side idle close is discovered on use, which marks the connection broken then.

items.name: acquire
items.sig: fn acquire(p: Pool, deadline: until) -> result[Conn, str]
items.doc: A connection for the caller's exclusive use, until release().

items.name: release
items.doc: Returns a connection to the pool. One that is broken, closed, or inside MULTI is closed instead: handing those to the next caller would fail its first command, or run it inside someone else's uncommitted transaction.

items.name: pool_do
items.doc: One command on a pooled connection: acquire, run, release. The connection goes back even when the command fails.

items.name: pool_close
items.doc: Closes every idle connection. Connections checked out are closed as they are released; acquire fails from now on. Closes every idle connection. Connections checked out are closed as they are released; acquire fails from now on.

items.name: new_cluster
items.doc: Connect to a cluster: try each seed until one serves CLUSTER SLOTS. Only database 0 exists in cluster mode. The deadline covers the whole bootstrap.

items.name: cluster_refresh
items.sig: fn cluster_refresh(cl: Cluster, deadline: until) -> result[bool, str]
items.doc: Re-learn the whole slot map from a known node (any current pool will do; the first one wins) or a bootstrap seed. Manual recovery for outages the MOVED path cannot see.

items.name: cluster_do
items.sig: fn cluster_do(cl: Cluster, key: str, args: [bytes],
items.doc: Run args against the node owning key, following MOVED (map update plus retry, up to MAX_REDIRECTS) and ASK (one directed ASKING hop, returned directly). Every other error returns verbatim.

items.name: multi
items.sig: fn multi(c: Conn, deadline: until) -> result[bool, str]
items.doc: MULTI: true on +OK. The connection leaves the pool from here until EXEC or DISCARD.

items.name: queue
items.doc: Queue one command inside MULTI. Anything but +QUEUED aborts the whole transaction server-side; that surfaces here as an err, and a later EXEC answers EXECABORT.

items.name: exec
items.sig: fn exec(c: Conn, deadline: until) -> result[[Reply], str]
items.doc: EXEC: the queued replies in order, error elements included. A nil array means nothing ran (watched keys changed): an err, since no caller could use an empty success. Always leaves MULTI, even on EXECABORT -- the server does too.

items.name: discard
items.sig: fn discard(c: Conn, deadline: until) -> result[bool, str]
items.doc: DISCARD: true on +OK, back outside MULTI either way the server answers.

items.name: watch
items.doc: WATCH/UNWATCH for optimistic locking: watch, read, MULTI, queue, EXEC; a nil EXEC (err here) means someone else wrote first, so retry the whole sequence.

items.name: evalsha
items.sig: fn evalsha(c: Conn, script: str, keys: [str], args: [bytes],
items.doc: EVALSHA with automatic EVAL fallback: the common path sends only 40 hex characters; a server that never saw the script answers NOSCRIPT and the call transparently re-sends the source.

items.name: Message
items.doc: A published message. kind is "message" or "pmessage"; pattern is set only for the latter (the glob that matched).

items.name: Sub
items.doc: A live subscription: a dedicated subscriber-mode connection plus messages that arrived while someone else held the lock. Never use sub.c directly (do, close, anything): concurrent socket readers would split the stream mid-reply. Everything here serializes on the Sub lock instead.

items.name: subscribe
items.doc: Subscribe, returning a live Sub. channels and patterns are the SUBSCRIBE and PSUBSCRIBE lists; at least one of them is nonempty.

items.name: sub_add
items.doc: Add subscriptions to a live Sub.

items.name: sub_next
items.sig: fn sub_next(sub: Sub, deadline: until) -> result[opt[Message], str]
items.doc: Next message, or none when the deadline passes first. Confirms and pongs the server interleaves are skipped, never surfaced; a malformed reply is an error, since valid RESP has only the shapes as_message knows.

items.name: sub_remove
items.doc: Remove subscriptions. Fully unsubscribing returns the connection to plain unicast mode; close it or subscribe again after.

items.name: sub_close
items.doc: Shut a subscription down. A task blocked in sub_next wakes with an error from the closed socket.
